title: India's Deadliest Heatwave in a Decade Has Killed at Least 77 People. Modi Just Warned the Nation. If You Are Planning a Summer Trip Home, You Need a Different Playbook.
excerpt: Temperatures have crossed 47°C in central India. Telangana alone has lost 52 people. Unofficial counts suggest 200 to 300 more. The India your parents describe from May is not the India that exists in May 2026.
body:
India is in the grip of its deadliest heatwave in at least a decade, and for the first time in years, the Prime Minister has stepped in personally to warn the country.

On May 27, Narendra Modi addressed the nation after India's top 45 cities all recorded temperatures above 43°C. Forest fires have erupted across multiple states. The Air Quality Index in several major metros has deteriorated sharply. And in the southern states of Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, heatstroke has killed at least 77 people — with unofficial estimates suggesting the real toll could be between 200 and 300.

The Numbers Are Staggering

Telangana alone has recorded 52 confirmed heatstroke fatalities. Andhra Pradesh has reported 25. Warangal district in Telangana has the highest toll at 23 deaths. The victims are disproportionately outdoor labourers, elderly residents, and pilgrims visiting temples during what is traditionally considered the summer pilgrimage season.

Vidarbha in Maharashtra hit 47.2°C — a temperature that causes organ failure in prolonged exposure. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has issued red alerts for Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, and adjoining regions, warning of continued extreme conditions through at least May 29.

Why This Year Is Different

India has always had hot summers. But 2026 is not a normal summer. The ongoing conflict in West Asia — specifically the Iran war that erupted on February 28 — has disrupted global energy supply chains. India, the world's third-largest oil importer, has been hit with four fuel price hikes in just ten days. Petrol has crossed ₹102 per litre in Delhi and ₹110 in Bengaluru. Diesel is nearing ₹100.

The cascading effect is brutal: higher fuel costs mean higher electricity costs, which mean more expensive air conditioning precisely when people need it most. Rural India, where power cuts are still routine, is absorbing the heat without reliable cooling.

Scientists are also pointing to a looming Super El Niño that could extend extreme heat patterns through June, July, and August — raising the spectre of a delayed or weakened monsoon.

What NRIs Planning Summer Trips Need to Know

If you are among the hundreds of thousands of Indian Americans planning a summer visit, the India you are about to step into is materially different from the one your parents described — or the one you remember from childhood visits.

The danger window has shifted. Heatstroke risk is no longer limited to midday. Doctors are reporting cases among people who ventured out at 9 AM or returned indoors at 5 PM. The traditional advice of "avoid the afternoon sun" is no longer sufficient when the ambient temperature at sunset is still 42°C.

Your parents may not recognise the risk. Elderly family members who have lived in India for decades often underestimate new heat extremes. The 77 confirmed deaths include multiple elderly individuals who were not performing heavy labour — they were simply going about their daily routines in temperatures their bodies could not handle.

Children are especially vulnerable. Paediatric heatstroke presentations have surged in hospitals across Telangana and Andhra Pradesh. If you are travelling with young children, outdoor time should be eliminated entirely between 10 AM and 5 PM.

Hydration alone is not enough. Health officials are advising ORS (oral rehydration salts) over plain water, wet cloth cooling for anyone who feels dizzy, and immediate hospital visits for anyone who stops sweating in extreme heat — a hallmark of severe heatstroke.

The Broader Pattern

India recorded its hottest year on record in 2024. The trend line has not reversed. Climate scientists from the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology have warned that extreme heat events in India are now occurring with a frequency that was not projected until the 2040s.

For the Indian diaspora, this is no longer an abstract climate story. It is a family safety story. The parents you left behind, the relatives who still walk to the temple at noon, the cousin whose workplace does not have air conditioning — they are living inside a heat emergency that is measurably more dangerous than anything India experienced a generation ago.

A Western Disturbance is expected to bring some relief to northern India from May 28 onward. For central and southern India, the forecast offers no reprieve until the monsoon arrives — and this year, even the monsoon's timing is uncertain.
